title: Emergency number (India)
text: In India, dial 112 for any emergency (police, fire, ambulance) from any phone. Use it if you or someone else is in immediate physical danger, being followed right now, or someone is trying to break in.

title: Women Helpline 181
text: 181 is the Women Helpline for women affected by violence, harassment or abuse. It offers listening support, information, and referral to police, shelters (One Stop Centres) and legal aid. Availability and hours can vary by state.

title: Women in distress police helpline 1091
text: 1091 is a police-linked helpline for women in distress, including harassment and stalking. Calls are routed to local police.

title: Reporting cybercrime: 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in
text: Online harassment, blackmail, fake profiles and threats to leak images can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in, which has a section for crimes against women and children where you may report with limited identity details. Helpline 1930 is mainly for financial cyber fraud. You can also file a complaint at a local police station or cyber cell.

title: Stopping spread of intimate images: StopNCII.org
text: StopNCII.org lets you create a digital fingerprint (hash) of an intimate image on your own device so participating platforms can block it from being shared. The image itself is not uploaded. It works for images that are threatened or already shared, if you have a copy. Platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and others also have their own reporting tools for non-consensual intimate images.

title: Threats to share private images (sextortion)
source: General safety guidance; verify with a legal-aid provider
text: Threatening to share private images to force contact, money or more images is a form of blackmail and image-based abuse. Common safety guidance: do not pay or send more, avoid meeting the person alone, keep the threats as evidence, and report to the platform and to cybercrime.gov.in. Complying often does not stop the threats.

title: Preserving evidence safely
text: Take screenshots showing the sender's name or number, date and time. Keep a dated log of incidents. Do not delete the original messages. Store copies where the other person cannot access them, such as a trusted friend's email or a new account with a password only you know. Consider whether the other person can see your phone, cloud backups or shared accounts.

title: Relevant Indian laws (overview)
text: Depending on facts, these may apply: stalking, voyeurism, criminal intimidation and sexual harassment under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS); publishing or transmitting private or obscene images electronically under the IT Act (e.g. sections 66E, 67, 67A); and domestic violence protection orders under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Exact section numbers and applicability should be confirmed with a lawyer or legal-aid service.

title: Free legal aid (NALSA, 15100)
text: Women are entitled to free legal services through State and District Legal Services Authorities. NALSA's helpline 15100 can connect you to legal aid. A legal aid lawyer can explain options like FIRs, protection orders and restraining orders before you decide anything.

title: Filing a complaint or FIR
text: You can approach the local police station or file online where available. For certain offences, police are expected to register an FIR. You may ask for a copy. Women can request that a woman officer record the statement. If a station refuses, senior police officers or a magistrate can be approached. Formal action can escalate the situation, so consider your safety and support first.

title: Domestic abuse: safety planning basics
text: Where it is safe, keep important documents (ID, bank details, medical records), some cash and a charged phone accessible. Identify a safe place and a trusted person. Know the quickest exit. One Stop Centres (Sakhi) offer shelter, medical, police and legal help in one place. Protection Officers under the PWDVA can help you seek protection orders.

title: Dealing with stalking
text: Keep a log of every incident with date, place and witnesses. Vary routines where possible, tell workplace security or neighbours, avoid direct engagement with the stalker, and check phones and vehicles for trackers or spyware. Report repeated following or contact to police; stalking is an offence.

title: Securing accounts and devices
text: Change passwords from a device the other person cannot access, turn on two-factor authentication, review logged-in devices, location-sharing and shared cloud accounts, and set social media to private. Be aware that sudden changes may alert an abusive person, so consider timing if you are living with them.

title: Talking to a trusted person
text: Telling a trusted friend, relative, colleague or counsellor can reduce isolation and give practical help like safe storage of evidence or a place to stay. Choose someone who will not pressure you, blame you, or confront the other person without your consent.

title: Mental health support: Tele-MANAS 14416
text: Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416) offers free, 24x7 mental health support in many languages. If someone is thinking of ending their life, they should also contact 112 or go to the nearest hospital.

title: NCW complaints
text: The National Commission for Women accepts complaints about harassment, domestic violence and other crimes against women, including online. It can take up cases with authorities and offers a helpline and online complaint portal.
